headline: High: Goose can write and exfiltrate from a shared filesystem while the zoomcamp repo is a non-runnable course artifact, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and compliance risks if paired in the same workspace.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a course repo with no runtime isolation or I/O surfaces, while agent B can read/write the filesystem and use MCP. If B opens files from the zoomcamp workspace, attacker-controlled content in those files could steer B’s tool use. The pathway is plausible but not proven by direct interaction evidence.
conditions: IF agent B reads files from the same workspace as agent A
IF agent A content is copied into prompts or MCP inputs without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the course repo and agent workspace directories
Disable automatic file-to-prompt ingestion for shared folders
Require provenance labels on any text B reads from A
Review MCP tool calls before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B has broad filesystem read/write and network egress, and agent A is a repository that may contain course materials or local files if co-located. Because B can transmit context to configured model providers, shared-workspace data could leak outward. Agent A itself has no egress, so the risk is driven by B’s default surfaces.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the same cwd as agent B
IF B sends file contents to configured model providers or MCP servers
mitigations: Keep sensitive files outside B’s working directory
Use a dedicated non-sensitive workspace for the pair
Restrict B’s provider keys and MCP servers to approved endpoints
Turn off automatic attachment of local files to prompts
Run a quick directory audit before starting B

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem, modify git state, and supports multiple instances with shared state via filesystem. Agent A is a repo artifact that may be edited or referenced in the same tree. Without locking, concurrent edits or git operations can overwrite each other; uncertainty about A’s runtime surfaces means we cannot rule this out, so severity stays high.
conditions: IF agent A and agent B operate in the same git checkout
IF two B instances or external edits touch the same files without locks
mitigations: Use separate clones for A and B
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Disable multi-instance editing in the shared repo
Commit or stash before starting another agent session
Review diffs after each agent completes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can act on filesystem and shell outputs, so if it treats agent A’s course content or generated text as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into edits or commands. Agent A is not runnable and does not itself verify outputs, so the main issue is B over-trusting A-derived content rather than a direct autonomous chain.
conditions: IF B uses A-produced text as instructions or facts without verification
IF B executes shell commands derived from A content
mitigations: Require a human check before executing A-derived commands
Ask B to summarize and verify A outputs before acting
Block direct command execution from pasted text
Use a checklist for any file edits sourced from A
Limit B to read-only mode during analysis

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B handles model-provider keys and extension tokens and can egress to configured providers, while agent A is a public course repo with no stated compliance controls. The pair can create policy mismatch if sensitive or regulated data is introduced into B’s workspace, but no specific residency or regulated-data class is documented for A, so this remains low.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent B’s workspace
IF provider or extension policies differ from the data’s residency requirements
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use only approved providers for B
Document retention settings before starting
Separate public course materials from sensitive projects
Review extension tokens and provider scopes
